extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of natural philosophy / scientific method (readers of Baconian induction and experimental physics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prescriptive instances for investigating the phenomenon of heat using Baconian induction: perform experiments, compare instances, apply methods of exclusion, and avoid preconceived forms. The text mixes specific experimental prescriptions about heat with general methodological rules for discovering 'forms' (causes) by exclusion and diligent experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer presence of heat from sensation alone
rubrics_metrics.description: We should be greatly deceived if we referred only to sensation as an indication of the presence of this cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between true heat and chemical stimulants that excite a sensation of heat (examples: quicklime, oil of vitriol). Note that some agents produce sensations or corrosion that are 'said' to burn, but are not necessarily the physical cause of heat; test by experiment rather than by vulgar parlance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish chemical corrosive/drying agents from actual heat
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of chemical agents, which from their corroding, blackening, dissolving, or drying up the parts of some bodies, and producing on them effects not generally unlike those produced by heat, are said in loose and vulgar language to burn them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether such agents become actually hot during action (e.g., combination with water causing heating). Do not conflate corrosive chemical action with thermal action; use experiments that measure real temperature changes or other indicators of heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate latent or potential heat in organic matter and soils
rubrics_metrics.description: Many organic matters (e.g., farm manures, cadavera) have latent and potential heat which may be collected by soils and can cause more rapid consumption/decomposition of newly buried corpses than pure earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare decomposition rates in different soils and contexts; experiment to detect 'latent' heat not directly perceptible to touch but manifest in effects (e.g., accelerated decay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate comparative heat across animals, species, and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire further into heat compared in different animals (fish, quadrupeds, serpents, birds) and according to species (e.g., lion, kite, man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make comparative measurements and observations: inter-species comparisons and intra-species (different organs and members) comparisons to determine relative degrees of heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure comparative heat in different organs of the same animal
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire further into heat compared in the same animal, according to parts and members; milk, blood, semen, eggs are found of a warm medical degree and less hot than the exterior flesh when moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to measure temperatures or effects in brain, stomach, heart, and other organs; do not assume uniform internal temperature without measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish celestial/astronomical contributions and test geometric factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun and planets are regarded to heat more when nearer (perigee) and when their rays fall more perpendicularly; conjunction with fixed stars and relative position may augment apparent heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test hypotheses about solar/planetary influence by controlled comparison of incidence angles (perpendicular vs oblique), distances (perigee/apogee), and conjunctions; beware of fanciful traditions and verify by experiment/observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify flames and ignitions by source and relative strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Flames and ignitions have many degrees in strength and weakness; flame from spirit of wine is soft; follow with flames from vegetable matter, wood, oil, tallow, resin, sulphur, camphor, naphtha, petroleum and salts after they are raw and broken up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform comparative combustion experiments to order flames by heating effect (not luminosity). Note editorial caution that Bacon's ordering may not match modern calorimetric results; measure heat output quantitatively where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mirrors/lenses to concentrate radiative heat and study focal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with burning mirrors: placing a mirror at different distances from a combustible object shows that motion (changing distance) augments the operation of heat though the cone and union of rays are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary focal length and distance systematically (span vs half-span example) and observe ignition intensity; verify role of motion/adjustment in focus and heating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate motion's effect on heat (including blowing, bellows, and relative motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion increases heat; seen in bellows and breath; harder motion increases operation of heat—e.g., tougher metals do not liquefy under still fire unless excited by motion (air supply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with forced air, bellows, and different rates of motion to quantify increases in combustion and temperature; consider explanation via oxygen supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Method of Exclusions / Rejection to discover forms (causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first work of true induction (for finding forms) is rejection or exclusion of natures: find instances where the nature sought is present without the given nature; or present when the given nature is absent; or increases when the given nature decreases; or decreases when the given nature increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and compare many instances (agreement and difference). Use the four kinds of instances (presence without given nature, absence with given nature, inverse variation) systematically to exclude candidate causes before affirming a 'form'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed from negatives (exclusion) to affirmatives only after exhaustive testing
rubrics_metrics.description: First perform rejection and exhaustive exclusion in due modes; then, after such rejections, will remain the affirmative form, solid and true. The mind should first proceed by negatives and finally end in affirmatives after all exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume causes prematurely; only endorse affirmative causal claims after comprehensive elimination of alternatives—recognize this requires many varied instances and is hard to fulfil fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of imposing accustomed human contemplations / preconceived forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat: do not draw those things which our contemplations and thoughts have hitherto accustomed us to, unto the forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid confirmation bias and intellectual habits that force data into familiar frameworks; keep rejection/exclusion strict and let data determine forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diligent, repeated experiment rather than trusting tradition or unverified reports
rubrics_metrics.description: We often insert 'fiat experimentum' and 'inquiratur ulterius' in many instances; our histories are poor unless experiments are made. Do not rely on tradition; perform experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever tradition or report suggests a phenomenon, perform controlled experiments to verify; repeat and vary conditions to test robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for plurality of causes; be cautious with Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to Plurality of Causes, the 'given nature' might be present without the other 'nature' even though the latter was one cause; the Method of Agreement is subject to imperfection arising from plurality of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using agreement/difference methods, consider that multiple causes may produce the same effect; aim for methods that control or eliminate plural causes (Double Method of Agreement/Difference) and seek exhaustive exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test effects of union and commixture of heats vs union of bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Union of different heats increases heat unless there is commixture of bodies; for example, a large focus and a small focus in the same place augment heat, but putting tepid water into boiling water cools it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between radiative/irradiance combination (which tends to add) and physical mixing of bodies (which can cool); design experiments accordingly (measure radiation vs mixed-body thermal equilibria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure material susceptibility to heat and heat retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of susceptibility: snow and ice melt with slight warmth; mercurial silver (argentum vivum) follows; oily bodies (oil, butter) then wood then water then stones and metals which do not easily heat (especially internally). Some bodies once heated retain heat long (e.g., hot iron/stone retains heat when plunged into cold water for a quarter of an hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify rates of warming and cooling, specific heats and conductivities; note that small bodies heat faster (mole effects) and that conduction requires time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller mass warms faster when brought near a hot body
rubrics_metrics.description: The smaller the mass of a body, the more quickly it warms when approximated to a hot body; this demonstrates that heat is in a manner tangible to bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for mass when comparing warming rates; design experiments comparing identical materials of different mass/size to isolate this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression or restriction of porous ignited materials extinguishes flame; structure matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In ignited porous substances—if space for motion of fire is shut by strong compression, the fire is extinguished (examples: crushed tow, candle wick pressed under a press or by foot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test the role of porosity and access to air/space for flame; design experiments applying compression to burning porous fuels and observe extinction thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flame behavior depends on concavity and available motion; certain explosive combustions are exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Flame will not be generated unless there is some concavity where flame can move and play, except in windy or powdered explosive cases where compression/incarceration increases flame fury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the geometrical/structural conditions for flame sustainment; study special cases (gunpowder, saltpetre) where confinement/pressure changes behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some heated but non-ignited systems can exceed flame temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: From things heated but not ignited, such as boiling water and air in reverberatories, some are found to surpass the heat of many flames and ignited bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure temperatures of heated but non-flaming media (steam, reverberatory heated air) and compare with flame temperatures using appropriate thermometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of flame relative to wind affects spread; flames sometimes move against the wind when wind is strong
rubrics_metrics.description: Fires made by a strong wind make greater progress against the wind than with it, because flame rebounds with more pernicious motion when the wind abates than it proceeds with an impelling wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study flame spread under varying wind directions and speeds; analyze aerodynamic and oxygen-supply explanations rather than accepting the fanciful reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for duration (mora) in heating effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of presence of a heat source increases total heating effect (mora corporis auget calorem): a focus warming a room for an hour heats more than for half an hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include time as a parameter in experiments; distinguish intensity from integrated heating over time; note that this differs for light (illumination does not integrate similarly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct simple instruments to observe air expansion/contraction as thermometer
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a glass 'vitrurn' ('vitrum calendare') experiment: heat a glass bulb, invert it into water and observe water rising into the bulb as the air inside contracts on cooling; append marked paper scale to observe expansions/contractions with weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build and use simple air-thermometers/thermoscopic devices to detect subtle changes of 'hot' and 'cold' in air, and compare with more refined senses (animal spirits) and tactile assessment; ensure the device allows air exchange or has a controlled seal as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold irritation of surroundings can increase internal heat (irritatio per frigidum augent calorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irritation by cold surroundings increases heat (example: when air or a rod is violently compressed or bent, it rebounds further in the contrary direction—analogy of exasperation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test how exposure to cold, sudden compression, or other irritative conditions affect measurable internal or surface temperatures (e.g., in tissues or materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize many grades of heat reception; even very small heats alter otherwise insensitive bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many degrees in susceptibility; even very small and slender heat alters and somewhat warms bodies that are least receptive, e.g., the heat of the hand slightly warms a lead shot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sensitive measurements to detect small thermal transfers and appreciate gradations of susceptibility across materials.
